papers.title: Microglial Stim1/Stim2 deletion reduces calcium signaling but promotes infarct expansion after ischemic stroke
papers.abstract: Microglia respond to ischemic stroke with calcium transients carried by calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels, gated by the endoplasmic reticulum sensors Stim1 and Stim2. Since CRAC signaling drives pro-inflammatory responses in immune cells, blocking it in microglia should protect the ischemic brain. We have examined this hypothesis in 15-month-old mice lacking Stim1 and Stim2 in microglia (Cx3cr1-CreERT2; Stim cKO). In vivo two-photon imaging confirmed that cKO microglia produced one-third smaller calcium transients during cortical spreading depolarizations. We then followed distal middle cerebral artery occlusion (dMCAo) with multiparametric MRI at 9.4 T. Six hours after occlusion, both the control and cKO genotypes demonstrated similar infarct size, edema, and diffusion, but lesion perfusion tended to be lower in cKO mice. Differences in tissue injury emerged later. Between 6 and 48 hours, the infarcts in control males did not grow, whereas infarcts in cKO males expanded 2.7-fold. At 48 hours, cKO males had 2.2-fold larger infarcts, while cKO females did not differ from controls. Moreover, cKO lesions showed a lower apparent diffusion coefficient, indicating more severe tissue injury. Neither hemispheric swelling nor cerebral arterial anatomy accounted for these differences. Contrary to our hypothesis, ablating microglial CRAC channels worsened stroke outcome. Microglial CRAC signaling may therefore protect threatened tissue in the first days after ischemia, possibly by sustaining its perfusion, and this role appears to outweigh its pro-inflammatory effects.

papers.title: Inactivation of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase reduces phosphatidylcholine amounts in the brain of infant mice
papers.abstract: Hypophosphatasia is a rare disease caused by dysfunctions of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase (TNAP). TNAP is expressed in numerous tissues, notably the brain, and patients with hypophosphatasia exhibit neurological symptoms, including epilepsy in the most severe forms of the disease. TNAP knockout (KO) mouse models have provided a wealth of information regarding TNAP functions. Specifically, metabolomic studies focusing on the aqueous fraction of the brain of TNAP KO mice identified numerous molecules whose amounts were altered as a direct or indirect consequence of TNAP inactivation. Among these molecules, several are involved either directly (e.g., vitamin B6) or indirectly (e.g., N-acetylaspartate) in lipid metabolism. In this study, we therefore extended these investigations by examining the consequences of TNAP inactivation on the brain lipidome. We used a targeted lipidomic approach, examining four main categories of lipids: fatty acids, neutral lipids, sphingolipids and glycerophospholipids, subdivided into 16 lipid classes and amounting to 296 lipid species. Eleven lipid species showed significantly reduced amounts in the brain of TNAP KO mice. All belonged to the phosphatidylcholine class. As phosphatidylcholines are major constituents of brain cell membranes, our results suggest that hypophosphatasia could be associated with alterations in membrane structure and functions, which could contribute to the neurodevelopmental disorders associated with the disease.

papers.title: Nucleus reuniens gates selective hippocampal-prefrontal interactions during NREM sleep
papers.abstract: Memory consolidation requires functional synchrony between the hippocampus (HC) and the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). The nucleus reuniens (RE) is a structural and functional hub between HC and mPFC. Here, we used in vivo electrophysiology to monitor the hippocampal-thalamic-prefrontal network in rats during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep. We identified ripple-like activity in the RE (120 Hz peak frequency, 45 ms oscillatory duration) that occurred most frequently during NREM sleep and was associated with robust recruitment of thalamic neural spiking. RE ripple activity was phase-locked to both hippocampal sharp wave-ripples (SWR) and mPFC ripples. Although ripples were independently detected in all three structures, we found that coupling between HC and mPFC ripples mainly involved co-occurring RE ripples. These results suggest RE ripples help organize when hippocampal activity engages prefrontal circuits during sleep, with potential implications for network mechanisms of memory consolidation.

papers.title: Repeated self-administered EEG recordings enable longitudinal measurement of brain activity at home
papers.abstract: Mobile electroencephalography (EEG) offers new opportunities to investigate brain activity outside the laboratory, but the quality and reliability of self-administered recordings remain important concerns. Here, we evaluated whether repeated at-home recordings using a four-channel consumer EEG device could provide meaningful electrophysiological measurements and characterized the stability of these measures across sessions. Five participants completed repeated recordings across multiple days, including resting-state measurements and an auditory oddball task performed with and without concurrent cognitive load. The recordings captured established spectral signatures of physiological state and task demands, including increased alpha activity during eye closure and changes in theta activity associated with cognitive load. Auditory stimulation elicited clear event-related responses, while exploratory multivariate decoding distinguished standard from target tones across recording sessions. Measurement stability varied across electrophysiological features, and aggregating repeated sessions improved the consistency of individual-level estimates. For example, split-half reliability of the auditory N1-like response increased from r = .22 with one session to r = .76 with seven sessions per half. By demonstrating the feasibility of repeated self-administered EEG measurements, this study provides a step toward investigating how brain activity varies both between individuals and within individuals over time in everyday environments.

papers.title: Electrophysiology of multisite direct electrical stimulation in the human brain
papers.abstract: Human cognition and neurological disorders reflect properties of distributed networks, yet how best to engage these networks therapeutically remains unknown. Multisite stimulation is a principled strategy for engaging brain networks, but a key translational barrier is understanding how a network combines concurrent inputs from multiple nodes. Here, we investigated the electrophysiology of simultaneous multisite direct electrical stimulation in 20 participants implanted with stereo-EEG electrodes. Synchronized dual-site stimulation engaged a larger effective network than single-site stimulation. Linear superposition explained most responses, but distinct nonlinear responses were also observed. Sublinear responses, consistent with saturation, occurred proximal to stimulation sites, while supralinear responses arose in network-connected sites during the response's late component. Moreover, low-intensity dual-site stimulation matched or exceeded single-site stimulation at higher intensities. These principles extended to three-site stimulation. These findings systematically characterize how responses to simultaneous multisite stimulation interact in the human brain, a foundational step towards principled, network-guided neurostimulation therapies.

papers.title: Amyloidosis and tauopathy progressively disrupt near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits
papers.abstract: Mechanistically distinct neurodegenerative diseases result in similar cognitive deficits, and pathology is often concentrated in a set of circuits known to be selectively vulnerable. Selective vulnerability is an intrinsic property of a circuit: in APP/PS1 mice, where plaques are global, functional disruptions are confined to circuits within the default mode network. What characterizes the dynamics of vulnerable circuits from those of spared circuits is unknown. We asked whether the distinguishing property is the proximity of population dynamics to criticality, a homeostatic set-point of network activity that determines computational capacity. We recorded single units simultaneously in three selectively vulnerable regions (retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and CA1 hippocampus) and in primary visual cortex of freely behaving young and old APP/PS1 and wild-type mice. Firing rate and spike-time variability differed by genotype inconsistently across regions and ages. In contrast, three measures from criticality theory each revealed deficits that emerged only with age and only in the vulnerable regions. No measure detected a progressive change in V1. Avalanche scaling is not fixed in neural activity, but varies along a scaling line as the network state changes. As a result, the lines generated by each genotype revealed a constitutive effect of the transgene in young animals, which inverted with age in amyloid-bearing animals, but only in vulnerable circuits. If the destabilization of near-critical dynamics directly reflects a circuit's functional capacity, the same signature should identify a mechanistically distinct degenerative disease. In a model of tauopathy (P301S/E4), CA1 dynamics were displaced from the control scaling line with the same age-dependent reversal observed in APP/PS1. Our results suggest a network-level principle of neurodegenerative diseases: molecularly unrelated pathologies converge on the loss of near-critical dynamics in selectively vulnerable circuits.

papers.title: Satellite glial translatome reprograms to favor mitochondrial and vesicular signaling under pelvic pain conditions
papers.abstract: Sensory satellite glial cells actively contribute to inflammatory and neuropathic pain, but their roles in pelvic pain remain unclear. This study examined how the active translating mRNAs in sensory SGCs change during pelvic pain symptoms using translating ribosome affinity purification followed by RNA sequencing (TRAP-seq) in a chronic pelvic pain (CPP) mouse model. Our data showed that SGCs exhibit sex-specific translatome patterns at baseline, which were reprogrammed in CPP conditions under the control of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (Eif4e). In CPP conditions, sensory SGCs exhibit increased translation of mitochondrial and vesicular genes and suppression of immune genes in both sexes; an anti-inflammatory cytokine profile was detected in female pelvic sensory ganglia. We are the first to characterize SGC translatome in pelvic pain conditions and to report sex differences in SGC translatome. Our data suggested that mitochondrial and vesicular gene translation in sensory SGCs may be important to afferent hypersensitivity.

papers.title: A Variational Principle for the Emergence of Neural Geometry Underlying Bayesian-Like Behavior
papers.abstract: Neural population geometry constrains how task variables are represented and read out into behavior. We propose a variational principle in which learning balances task accuracy and representational smoothness under stimulus-dependent weighting. This balance links stimulus statistics to the shape of a latent neural coordinate. For magnitude estimation, the principle predicts distortions near the edges of bounded ensembles, global affine contraction for Gaussian ensembles, and warping toward high-probability regions for bimodal ensembles. We test the bounded-uniform case in recurrent neural networks trained to reproduce time intervals. Their learned geometries occupy three regimes as the boundary distortions change from too narrow to resolve, to measurable, to extending across the stimulus range. A shape parameter selected from an empirical neural coordinate predicts the nonlinear component of mean behavior through an affine readout, with only behavioral gain and offset fitted afterward. In this bounded-uniform setting, the variational coordinate and Bayesian least-squares mean response have closely matching shapes after affine normalization. These results suggest a variational account of how stimulus statistics shape neural geometry and yield Bayesian-like behavior.

papers.title: Zdhhc17/Hip14 functions in neurons to control behavior via DHHC-dependent and independent mechanisms
papers.abstract: To navigate a complex sensory environment, animals filter out inconsequential sensory inputs and habituate to familiar stimuli. By establishing innate response thresholds and modifying them through habituation, animals can focus on key sensory stimuli while ignoring irrelevant ones. Huntingtin-interacting protein 14 (Hip14), also known as zDHHC17, is a palmitoyl acyltransferase (PAT) that regulates both of these sensory filtering processes. Larval zebrafish lacking Hip14 are hypersensitive to acoustic stimuli and cannot regulate their responses to repeated acoustic stimuli via habituation. Yet how Hip14 regulates these behaviors, and whether it does so through different mechanisms, is unknown. Prior work demonstrates that Hip14 is expressed throughout the nervous system, but where it functions to control these overlapping sensory functions remains unaddressed. We found that the catalytic (DHHC) domain, despite being a defining feature for PATs including Hip14, is not required for regulating acoustic startle sensitivity, but is sufficient to regulate habituation. We find, furthermore, that Hip14 function in either mechanosensory hair cells or neurons can restore normal startle sensitivity, whereas habituation is regulated exclusively by neuronal expression. Finally, we found that the Hip14 N-terminal ankyrin repeat domains are crucial for its control of behavior. Together, our study establishes that habituation and startle sensitivity are regulated through distinct circuit and molecular mechanisms and establishes a new in vivo catalytic-independent role for Hip14.

papers.title: Neural dynamics track the approach to physical exhaustion
papers.abstract: Physical exhaustion has long been described through its cardiorespiratory and metabolic cost, while the neural dynamics of its approach remain largely unexplored. Here we recorded high-density electroencephalography in 28 trained cyclists during a maximal incremental test to characterise how neural dynamics change towards exhaustion. As physiological strain rose, oscillatory power shifted to lower frequencies, neural activity became more regular and predictable, and functional coupling extended to longer timescales. Participant-specific models built on neural dynamics tracked proximity to exhaustion with accuracy comparable to cardiorespiratory measures. Over the final minutes, neural features remained informative while cardiorespiratory measures lost accuracy. Models trained across participants still tracked proximity to exhaustion, but less precisely. The approach to exhaustion thus follows a common neural path, tuned to each individual.

papers.title: Neuronal Aralar/AGC1 deficiency impairs social behavior through dopaminergic and redox dysfunction and is rescued by β-hydroxybutyrate
papers.abstract: Background: Pathogenic variants in SLC25A12/AGC1 (Aralar) have been linked to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the mechanisms connecting neuronal metabolic dysfunction to altered social behavior remain poorly understood. Aralar is a key component of the malate-aspartate shuttle, supporting neuronal oxidative metabolism and lactate utilization. Here, we investigated the consequences of postnatal neuronal Aralar deletion and the therapeutic potential of {beta}-hydroxybutyrate (BHB). Methods: We generated neuron-specific Aralar knockout mice (Neu Aralar-KO) using CamKII-Cre, producing efficient recombination in cortex, hippocampus, and striatum. Behavioral, transcriptomic, neurochemical, morphometric, histological, and biochemical analyses were performed in adult mice. The effects of systemic BHB administration were assessed using behavioral, metabolic, oxidative stress, and transcriptomic endpoints. Results: Despite a 55-65% reduction of Aralar expression in forebrain regions, Neu Aralar-KO mice displayed normal growth, survival, brain structure, and myelination. Unexpectedly, loss of neuronal Aralar did not impair spatial memory, episodic memory, or reversal learning. In contrast, Neu Aralar-KO mice exhibited hyperactivity and a marked deficit in sociability, revealing an ASD-relevant behavioral phenotype. Morphological analysis showed significant remodeling of striatal dendritic spines without changes in spine density. Transcriptomic profiling identified 433 differentially expressed genes, the vast majority being upregulated, with enrichment of pathways related to neuropeptide signaling, synaptic transmission, membrane excitability, and behavior. Notably, genes involved in dopamine (DA) and glutamate handling, synaptic connectivity, neuromodulatory signaling, and ASD-associated pathways were strongly induced. Neurochemical analyses revealed preserved glutamate and GABA levels but reduced striatal DA content accompanied by an increased DOPAC/DA ratio, indicating enhanced DA degradation. DAergic neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) showed minimal recombination, suggesting that DA dysfunction arises through non-cell-autonomous mechanisms. Consistent with increased DA oxidative catabolism, Neu Aralar-KO striata displayed elevated lipid peroxidation, induction of glutathione-related pathways, upregulation of antioxidant genes, and astrocyte activation. Remarkably, BHB treatment restored sociability, normalized striatal metabolic alterations, reduced oxidative stress, and abolished genotype-dependent neurochemical abnormalities. Transcriptomic analyses further revealed that Aralar deficiency recapitulates a substantial fraction of the fasting/BHB-induced epigenetic transcriptional program. Conclusions: Postnatal neuronal Aralar deficiency uncouples social behavior from cognitive performance and drives ASD-like phenotypes through a mechanism linking neuronal metabolic dysfunction, oxidative stress, glial activation, and impaired DAergic homeostasis. The rescue of behavioral, metabolic, and redox abnormalities by BHB identifies restoration of metabolic homeostasis as a major therapeutic mechanism and highlights metabolic interventions as promising strategies for AGC1 deficiency and ASD-associated disorders involving neuronal metabolic dysfunction.

papers.title: TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction and Clustering From Sparse Evidence For Disease Subtyping and Staging
papers.abstract: Chronic progressive diseases often follow heterogeneous courses, with individuals differing in the pattern and timing of biomarker abnormalities. However, observed data are typically sparse and predominantly cross-sectional, with limited follow-up covering only short segments of disease progression. Reconstructing heterogeneous trajectories from such data requires disentangling variation along disease trajectories from subtype heterogeneity while inferring individuals' unknown subtype assignments and disease stages. Existing approaches may confound disease stage with subtype, scale poorly as the number of biomarkers increases, or fail to effectively integrate cross-sectional and longitudinal observations. We propose TRACE: Trajectory Reconstruction And Clustering from Sparse Evidence, a probabilistic framework that jointly reconstructs biomarker trajectories and infers disease subtypes and continuous stages. TRACE combines monotonic neural networks for flexible modeling and data-driven clustering of subtype-specific progression trajectories with temporal regularization derived from longitudinal observations when available. All model components are jointly optimized end to end using stochastic gradient descent, enabling efficient and scalable estimation. We evaluate TRACE on semi-simulated MRI biomarker data with known subtype and stage structures and demonstrate its ability to identify clinically meaningful subtypes and disease stages in real-world neurodegenerative disease datasets.

papers.title: Selective ultrasonic suppression of pathological brain hyperactivity via an endogenous CAV3-NCX1 axis
papers.abstract: Selective suppression of pathological hyperactivity is a major therapeutic challenge across brain disorders. Ultrasound stimulation can modulate neural activity, yet the molecular basis of its inhibitory effects and its ability to selectively inhibit hyperactive rather than basally active cells remain unclear. Here, we identify the caveolin-3 (CAV3)-sodium-calcium exchanger-1 (NCX1) complex as a previously unknown mediator of state-dependent ultrasound-induced neural inhibition. Prolonged ultra-low-intensity ultrasound stimulation engages NCX1-mediated Ca2+ extrusion in hyperactive neurons and astrocytes, sparing cells with basal activity. NCX1 is both necessary and sufficient for this inhibitory response, and disruption of the CAV3-NCX1 interface abolishes the ultrasound-induced effects. In vivo, targeted ultrasound stimulation suppresses fear-evoked hyperactivity and freezing in an NCX1-dependent manner and attenuates neuropathic pain-associated hyperactivity, allodynia, and hippocampal epileptiform activity. These findings establish a molecular mechanism for state-dependent ultrasound inhibition, providing a basis for a new approach to neuromodulation that selectively targets pathological hyperactivity.

papers.title: Non-invasive temporal interference stimulation targeting the hippocampus enhances fast motor memory consolidation
papers.abstract: Converging neuroimaging evidence indicates that the hippocampus is involved in motor sequence learning (MSL) and its consolidation at multiple timescales. However, direct evidence for a causal role of the hippocampus in these processes in healthy humans remains scarce, partly due to the inability of conventional non-invasive brain stimulation techniques to reach this deep brain structure. Here, we used temporal interference stimulation (TIS) - a technique enabling non-invasive stimulation targeted toward deep brain regions - to probe the functional role of the hippocampus in MSL and its consolidation. In two separate experiments, sixty-four young healthy adults (36 females) received, in within-subject counterbalanced designs, active (5 Hz envelope) or control (0 Hz envelope) hippocampal-targeted TIS either during active practice of an MSL task (task-TIS experiment, n = 32) or during the short rest periods interleaved with task practice known to support rapid forms of consolidation (rest-TIS experiment, n = 32). Consolidation was assessed at both the micro timescale (i.e., over the short "micro-offline" rest intervals interspersed with task practice) and macro timescale (i.e., over a 24-hour "macro-offline" retention interval). Our results indicate that TIS targeting the hippocampus during inter-practice rest periods - but not during task practice - significantly enhanced micro-offline gains in performance as compared to control stimulation. While this effect did not carry over to the 24-hour retention interval at the group level, participants with greater stimulation-induced micro-offline gains showed larger overnight performance improvements. These findings provide the first direct evidence that experimental interventions targeting the hippocampus modulate offline motor memory consolidation processes.

papers.title: State-Dependent Stimulation for Seizure Termination in a Morris-Lecar Network: A Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: The efficacy of neurostimulation for seizure termination depends not only on the stimulus itself but also on the dynamical state of the epileptic network. Here, we develop a dynamical-systems-informed reinforcement-learning framework that learns when to deliver a predefined pulse to terminate seizure-like activity. We simulate a sparsely connected network of 100 extended three-dimensional Morris-Lecar neurons. Bifurcation analysis of the single-neuron model identifies bistable regimes and provides a mechanistic basis for considering transitions between resting and oscillatory activity. The learning agent uses semi-gradient Q-learning with tile coding and receives a two-dimensional time-delay embedding of either the population-averaged membrane potential or a derivative-based proxy for extracellular potential. It learns a state-dependent policy that selects between stimulation and no stimulation, without modifying the pulse waveform. Across 30 independently generated test networks, both learned policies markedly reduced median seizure duration compared with trigger-only and state-independent stimulation controls. The two learned policies performed comparably, indicating that the estimated extracellular potential proxy retained sufficient dynamical information for control in this model. These results provide a proof of concept that combining dynamical-systems-based state reconstruction with online reinforcement learning can identify effective stimulation timing for terminating seizure-like activity.

papers.title: Combining non-linear and spectral cardiac variability metrics differentiates rat alcohol drinking with and without challenge
papers.abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remains a substantial global challenge, with notable individual and sex differences. Heart rate variability (HRV) offers a potential link into the autonomic system underlying alcohol drinking. While simpler, time-domain HRV metrics have been explored, non-linear indicators could provide unique insights into more complex states like compulsive drinking, intake that persists despite negative consequences. We examined heart rate traces from male and female rats during intake of alcohol-only and alcohol+10mg/L quinine, a putative compulsive drinking model. In particular, we re-analyzed previously published findings, but newly focused on several non-linear HRV metrics: the Poincare ratio (possibly reflecting sympathovagal balance) and MultiScale entropy (MSE, perhaps reflecting unpredictability in broader and narrower time windows), along with the previously unexamined spectral HRV metrics (the parasympathetic indictor high-frequency HRV, HF-HRV%). HRV was assessed for the first ~1100 heart beats (~2.5 minutes), to assess HRV correlates of greater alcohol front-loading while having approximately similar amount of data per session. Lower Poincare ratio and higher HF-HRV% were overall related to higher alcohol consumption. In contrast, compulsive drinking, but not alcohol-only, was associated with lower broader-window HRV entropy, which was more pronounced in males. Drinking- and sex-related patterns were further identified using Principle Component Analysis, Ordinary Least Squares, and Linear Mixed Models. Limitations included perhaps being underpowered to detect significant relationships, especially in females. Thus, our preliminary findings suggest that combining HRV metrics could represent useful biomarkers for consumption levels during front-loading, which distinguished general intake from compulsion.

papers.title: Impaired cholinergic modulation of striatal spiny projection neurons in repetitive behaviors associated with TSHZ3-linked autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: Alterations in central cholinergic systems are implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We previously identified TSHZ3 as an ASD-linked gene and provided evidence, from transgenic mouse models, supporting the view that striatal cholinergic interneurons (SCINs) are key players in the core ASD trait represented by repetitive behaviors (RBs). Indeed, conditional deletion of Tshz3 in cholinergic neurons (Chat-cKO model) results in RBs associated with reduced SCIN firing activity and decreased striatal cholinergic tone. Here we tackled the resulting adaptations in the striatal circuitry underlying RBs in Chat-cKO, focusing on the two populations of striatal projection neurons (SPNs) that express dopamine D1 (D1R) or D2 (D2R) receptor. Using patch-clamp electrophysiological recordings, as well as behavioral, pharmacological and molecular approaches, we show reduced cholinergic transmission through the muscarinic M1 receptor onto SPNs, with no changes in the functionality or expression of this receptor. Notably, we demonstrate a loss of the differential excitability of D1R- vs. D2R-SPNs. Finally, acute in vivo treatment with the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor donepezil significantly alleviates RBs in mutant mice. These findings point to dysfunction of SCINs as a pathological and druggable mechanism underlying RBs in Tshz3-linked ASD, and to altered SPN excitability as a critical contributor in the resulting pathophysiological functioning of the striatum.

papers.title: Direction of oscillatory networks in the human medial temporal lobe reverses across verbal working memory phases
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) requires neural circuits to change how they interact as information is encoded, maintained and used. Directional oscillatory interactions in the medial temporal lobe (MTL) contribute to memory processing, but how these interactions are spatially organized during verbal WM remains unclear. Here, we analyzed intracranial electroencephalogram and neuronal spiking recorded from the human MTL during a verbal Sternberg task. Theta- and gamma-band activities in MTL showed predominant directionality in the posterior-to-anterior axis during WM encoding, but this direction was reversed to anterior-to-posterior during retrieval. Theta activities reflecting the WM load were more prevalent in left than right MTL, and theta in left MTL coordinated spike timings more strongly. Moreover, interhemispheric interactions showed a predominant left-to-right influence, with posterior-to-anterior interactions enhanced during encoding and anterior-to-posterior interactions enhanced during retrieval. Together, these findings suggest that verbal WM engages a spatially organized MTL network in which the predominant direction of oscillatory interactions changes across task phases.

papers.title: Daily light exposure differences between extreme chronotypes persist after alignment to habitual sleep timing
papers.abstract: Purpose: Morning and evening chronotypes may receive light at different clock times, thereby providing differently timed signals to the circadian pacemaker. Prior studies have suggested phase-specific exposure patterns that could counter further advances in early types and delays in late types. We examined whether photoperiod modifies these exposure patterns in a way that could reasonably counteract timing extremes. Methods: We analysed near-eye melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (EDI) in 140 participants from an international cohort across seven countries (778 participant-days; 35,949 half-hour observations). We compared four quartiles of midsleep on free days corrected for sleep debt (MSFsc) in clock time and relative to MSFsc using cyclic generalized additive mixed models, accounting for day type, site, photoperiod and individual patterns. In exploratory analyses, we tested moderation of these differences by daylength and used phase-response-curve (PRC) weighting as a conceptual comparison of exposure timing. Results: The modelled extreme evening-type/morning-type exposure ratios averaged 0.16 (95% CI 0.06-0.40) 9.6-11.3 hours before MSFsc (pre-MSFsc) and 14.0 (5.6-34.8) 0.9-4.4 hours after MSFsc (post-MSFsc). The models performed similarly well by ordinary in-sample R2 (0.795 for clock time; 0.794 for MSFsc-relative time). Pattern differences were broadly similar on work and free days, with the pre-MSFsc contrast descriptively attenuated on free days. The post-MSFsc ratio increased by a factor of 2.59 (95% CI 1.06-6.34) between civil photoperiods one hour below and above each site's average photoperiod, with no significant moderation of the pre-MSFsc contrast. Exploratory weighting by the published PRC gave higher advance-weighted point estimates in extreme evening than extreme morning types; the group difference was not statistically significant. Conclusions: Extreme chronotypes differ in daily exposure both in clock time and relative to MSFsc. The established questionnaire-based MSFsc measure showed significant post-MSFsc daylength moderation. The exposure patterns and conceptual PRC comparison suggest a possible pathway linking daylight availability to entrainment in extreme chronotypes.

papers.title: The Xist locus on the X chromosome of males regulates cognition and metabolism despite minimal expression
papers.abstract: The long non-coding RNA Xist is the master regulator of X chromosome inactivation (XCI) in females, but its functional significance in males, where Xist expression is normally minimal, is unknown. Here we investigated whether the Xist locus influences male physiology and brain function across the lifespan using mice carrying a targeted Xist deletion ({Delta}Xist). Xist deletion produced a small further reduction in the very low, residual Xist signal in aged male hippocampus. Metabolically, Xist deletion lowered fasting blood glucose in old, not young, males, without affecting body weight. In the brain, Xist deletion modestly improved spatial memory at 24 hours in the Morris water maze in young males, with a similar trend at middle age in an interactive place avoidance task, independent of anxiety-like behavior or locomotor activity. This early cognitive benefit did not persist with aging and motor function on the rotarod was unaffected by genotype at any age. Together, these findings indicate that the Xist locus exerts age- and domain-specific effects on male metabolic and cognitive functions despite near-absent baseline Xist expression. These data identify an unexpected role for a canonically female-associated regulatory locus in males and raise the possibility that Xist-associated mechanisms contribute to male brain function and metabolism.

papers.title: Single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of 5xFAD mouse brain maps cell-type-specific transcriptional disruption and preferential rolipram rescue in VIP interneurons
papers.abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease is characterized by progressive synaptic dysfunction and inhibitory circuit disruption across multiple brain cell types. Rolipram, a selective phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitor that elevates intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), activates proteasome, and produces robust procognitive effects in AD mouse models. Still, the cell-type-specific transcriptional mechanisms underlying these effects remain uncharacterized. Methods: We profiled 29,664 nuclei from 5xFAD and wild-type (WT) mouse right hemisphere across four conditions: WT Vehicle, WT Rolipram, 5xFAD Vehicle, and 5xFAD Rolipram (0.03 mg/kg/day, 30-day subcutaneous osmotic pump) using the Parse Biosciences Evercode WT v3 combinatorial barcoding platform. Nuclei were clustered into 16 annotated cell type populations using Seurat v5. Disease and rescue effects were quantified as log fold changes (LFCs) across all clusters, with Gene Ontology enrichment assessed using clusterProfiler and transcription factor activity inferred using decoupleR. Results: Disease-associated transcriptional disruption was highly cell-type-specific in its magnitude. Among inhibitory subtypes, VIP/Reln disinhibitory interneurons (n = 149 nuclei) showed the most coherent transcriptional disruption: 289 candidate genes were lower in 5xFAD, with Gene Ontology enrichment concentrated in synapse organization programs, including regulation of synapse structure or activity (padj = 1.5x10^-14, 44 genes), regulation of synapse organization (padj = 1.9x10^-14, 43 genes), and postsynapse organization (padj = 1.1x10^-13, 38 genes). This pathway-level specificity was not reproduced in PVALB or SST interneurons. Astrocytes showed loss of cell-adhesion programs (cell-substrate adhesion padj = 2.4x10^-4, 10 genes). Rolipram rescue was preferential: VIP interneurons yielded 72 true rescue genes and astrocytes yielded 42, with the remaining 14 clusters showing substantially fewer. The cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde7b was disease-context-specifically lower in 5xFAD VIP interneurons (LFC -0.53) and restored by rolipram (LFC +0.54), with WT expression unchanged. decoupleR CREB1 activity inference identified reduced CREB1 activity in 5xFAD VIP interneurons with partial restoration in 5xFAD Rolipram, supporting a stepwise transcriptional cascade in which amyloid pathology reduces cAMP, which suppresses PKA and CREB1 activity. This in turn reduces Pde7b transcription, and rolipram reverses this cascade by blocking cAMP hydrolysis upstream. Conclusion: This single-nucleus atlas provides the first cell-type-resolved characterization of rolipram's transcriptional effects in the 5xFAD brain. VIP disinhibitory interneurons emerge as the most transcriptionally vulnerable inhibitory subtype and the preferential site of rolipram-associated rescue, with the Pde7b/CREB1 signaling axis nominating a tractable, disease-context-specific pharmacological substrate.

papers.title: Probabilistic mapping of brain connections without random sampling
papers.abstract: For two decades, most tractography has mapped brain connections by sampling millions of pathways probabilistically. Sampling makes results non-deterministic and costly to store. We show that it is unnecessary: modeling tractography as an absorbing Markov chain gives the expected result of infinitely many streamlines. This approach is more reliable than streamline-based tractography across test--retest scans. It readily maps tracts in clinical-grade data and neonates, around tumors and along small pathways. MPAT is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rokemlab/mpat .

papers.title: State-dependent structure-function coupling reflects dynamic engagement of the brain's structural scaffold
papers.abstract: Functional brain organization is shaped by the brain's anatomical scaffold, yet how structure-function coupling varies across cognitive states remains unclear. Across 723 adults from two independent cohorts, we examined coupling using diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging. In the primary cohort, coupling was strongest during movie-watching, intermediate during rest, and weakest during working memory, declining further with increasing working-memory load. The movie-rest difference replicated in an independent sample, challenging the primacy of rest for revealing anatomical constraints. State effects were superimposed on a stable unimodal-to-transmodal cortical hierarchy, with movie-watching preferentially enhancing coupling in sensory and language systems. Regions with more stable functional connectivity across states showed stronger coupling. Older age was associated with lower auditory and somatomotor coupling in both cohorts, alongside heterogeneous increases in association cortex. Together, we show that cognitive context shapes structure-function alignment, supporting a framework of complementary structure-constrained and distributed-integrative modes of communication.

papers.title: Excitatory neurons downregulate synaptic proteins before motor onset and glia reduce neuronal support in Huntington disease mice
papers.abstract: Background: Huntington's disease burdens protein homeostasis and affects neurons and glia differently across brain regions, but how these two main cell populations respond as the disease progresses remains unresolved. Whole-tissue proteomes mix these cell types and hide how the proteome of each changes. We therefore measured the proteome of each cell type separately at different disease stages. Methods: We metabolically labelled cell-type-specific proteomes in living R6/1 mice and wild-type littermates for 15 days at different disease stages. We examined cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons at 1.5, 3 and 7 months, cerebellar inhibitory neurons at 3 and 7 months, and cortical, striatal and cerebellar glia at 7 months. We combined mass spectrometry with functional enrichment and competitive protein-set tests to understand the differential proteostatic response to mutant huntingtin across disease progression, brain regions and cell types. Differential abundance was tested with a peptide-centric linear mixed model (msqRob, Benjamini-Hochberg q < 0.1), and proteins whose levels varied together in cortical and hippocampal neurons were grouped into modules by weighted correlation network analysis. Results: Hippocampal excitatory neurons showed broader and more coordinated regulation than cortical neurons already before motor onset, whereas the cortical response increased with age and no cortical protein module differed between genotypes before the most severe stage. All three neuronal populations upregulated ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) proteins as the disease advanced. Protein folding changed, with more subunits of the chaperonin CCT/TRiC but fewer J-domain proteins and, in excitatory neurons, fewer HSP70 chaperones. At the most severe stage, glia of the three studied regions regulated mainly different proteins, but all increased UPS proteins and decreased key proteins of neuronal support, among them the main glial glutamate transporter GLT-1. Cholesterol-related proteins decreased in cortical and cerebellar glia, and respiratory-chain proteins in striatal glia. Conclusions: Synaptic proteins decreased early in cortical and hippocampal neurons and were not restored at later ages. A later and broader maintenance response coexisted with their continued and increasing downregulation. In this first cell-type-resolved view of the labelled proteome in a Huntington's disease mouse model, progression appears as a change in the coordination of cellular functions, which whole-tissue measurements would dilute.

papers.title: Identifying aligned tensor decompositions across heterogeneous neural datasets
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural recordings increasingly span many sessions, brain regions and animals, but differences in neuronal sampling make it difficult to identify and interpret shared patterns. We introduce Neuralign, a tensor- based model that jointly aligns and decomposes recordings into components, each pairing a shared temporal pattern with its expression in individual trials and neurons, without requiring matched neurons, matched trials or behavioural labels. In simulations, pooling recordings improved recovery of shared components; in recurrent networks, Neuralign distinguished related from distinct task solutions. In the macaque motor cortex, label-free components recovered the ring-like organisation of reach directions. Across 93 brain-wide mouse recordings, Neuralign discovered a single component that isolated the response to inhibition of the anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM). A reference learned from correct, uninhibited trials revealed inhibition-related activity outside the choice direction on error trials, most strongly in the ALM and thalamus. Neuralign provides an interpretable framework for studying the shared structure of large neural datasets, linking shared patterns to individual trials and recorded populations.

papers.title: Neural and Experiential Dynamics of High-Ventilation Breathwork Mirror Psychedelic States
papers.abstract: High-ventilation breathwork (HVB) is a simple breathing technique that nevertheless frequently triggers experiences resembling psychedelic states. While recent studies have begun to pinpoint physiological and neural changes involved in altered states of consciousness (ASCs) evoked by HVB, the interplay between neural and experiential dynamics throughout an HVB session remains unclear. Here we tracked neural activity (via 64-channel EEG recordings) as well as subjective experience depth and content in 25 experienced HVB practitioners across resting-state recordings interleaved throughout a naturalistic HVB session. We find that neural dynamics evoked by HVB emulate the most robust neural signatures of classical psychedelic states, specifically (1) loosening of temporal structure, including broadband cortical desynchronization, increased signal complexity, and decreased oscillatory power in the Alpha (8 - 13 Hz) range, and (2) reorganization of spatial structure, including a flattening of cortical processing hierarchy. These neural effects directly correlated with participants subjective depth with minute resolution, but were not explained by isolated features of HVB such as music listening or active interoception. Together, these results identify unifying neural features of psychedelic-like ASCs regardless of induction method, demonstrating that cortical states triggered by psychedelics can also be accessed by non-pharmacological routes, and breathwork is a powerful way to do so.

papers.title: Single-Session HRV Biofeedback Alters Neural Activity but Not Subjective Anxiety
papers.abstract: Anxiety and stress are among the most prevalent mental health concerns worldwide, yet barriers to effective treatment remain high. Biofeedback-based approaches offer a promising, low-cost complement to traditional interventions. The present study examined whether real-time heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback enhances the efficacy of paced breathing for reducing state anxiety, and whether self-reported and neural measures of anxiety relief converge. Healthy adults completed a speeded Stroop task for stress induction, followed by a ten-minute paced breathing exercise. Participants were randomly assigned to an HRV biofeedback condition, in which real-time cardiac variability was displayed, or a control condition with the same breathing cue and no physiological feedback. State anxiety was assessed using the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S), and neural activity was measured via EEG spectral power across delta, theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands. The Stroop task reliably elevated state anxiety, and paced breathing reduced STAI-S scores equivalently in both groups; HRV biofeedback did not confer additional subjective benefit. In contrast, EEG analyses revealed that the biofeedback group showed increases in delta and bilateral theta power relative to controls, and spatially widespread increases in alpha and beta power. Time-frequency analyses further showed more extensive and sustained spectral modulation in the biofeedback condition. These findings reveal a dissociation between self-reported and neural responses to a brief HRV biofeedback intervention: paced breathing alone was sufficient to reduce acute state anxiety, while HRV biofeedback produced distinct changes in neural oscillatory activity without enhancing self-reported anxiety relief. These results show that subjective anxiety recovery and neural recovery can diverge during acute HRV biofeedback, suggesting that physiological engagement with biofeedback emerges before conscious benefits.

papers.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction activates a translational stress response that drives diabetic pain
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain is common and debilitating among diabetics. The reactive glycolytic metabolite methylglyoxal (MGO) is strongly associated with painful diabetic neuropathy. MGO triggers pain through activation of the integrated stress response (ISR). The underlying molecular mechanisms are unclear. Here, we show that general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) kinase acts as a conserved sensor that bridges glycolytic and mitochondrial dysfunction to pain hypersensitivity. In human sensory neurons derived from dorsal root ganglion (DRG), MGO increased eIF2 phosphorylation and suppressed global translation. These effects were blocked upon inhibition of GCN2. Unbiased ribosome profiling of mouse DRG revealed that MGO triggered repression of mRNAs that encode components of the electron transport chain. Based on this observation, mitochondrial dysfunction was examined as a potential upstream trigger for GCN2 activation. MGO directly glycated mitochondrial complex I and increased the NADH/NAD+ ratio. Correcting this redox imbalance via expression of a mitochondrial-targeted bacterial NADH oxidase (mitoLbNOX) prevented ISR activation by MGO. In a streptozotocin-induced mouse model of diabetic neuropathy, pharmacological GCN2 inhibition or sensory neuron-specific conditional deletion significantly attenuated mechanical allodynia. Calcium imaging revealed that genetic deletion of GCN2 reduced calcium influx in response to an agonist of TRPA1. Finally, expression of mitoLbNOX using adeno-associated viruses (AAV) in DRG sensory neurons in vivo reduced streptozotocin-induced mechanical hypersensitivity. Our findings demonstrate that GCN2 is a central, conserved driver of translational dysregulation downstream of mitochondrial redox stress in diabetic pain. This work highlights the critical role of mitochondrial function and translational control as key drivers of painful diabetic neuropathy.

papers.title: Aging limits the reduction of reactive muscle activity to perturbations but spares the retrieval of context-specific patterns with practice
papers.abstract: Moving smoothly through a changing environment requires immediate reactive responses to maintain balance at an environmental transition, and learned, context-specific responses to efficiently meet the new environmental demands. People use both the reactive and context-specific responses to adapt to new environment and to re-adapt more rapidly on subsequent re-encounters. While re-adaptation slows with older age, the underlying muscular mechanisms are unknown. We hypothesized that practice would reduce reactive recruitment and increase context-specific recruitment and that both changes would be smaller in older adults. To test this, younger and older adults practiced split-belt walking (one belt faster than the other) over three days. We recorded surface electromyography from 10 muscles per leg and used linear regression to decompose each session's activity into a reactive component (template from naive, early exposure) and a context-specific component (template from practiced activity). Mixed-effects models showed that, with practice, older adults decreased reactive recruitment less than younger adults, particularly in distal muscles, with no strong evidence for an age difference in context-specific recruitment. In sum, with practice, aging limits the reduction of reactive responses to a novel walking context but spares the retrieval of context-specific muscle patterns, suggesting that mobility rehabilitation for older adults could target reactive mechanisms.

papers.title: A Dual Effort Choice paradigm reveals pharmacological divergence between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation within the same task environment
papers.abstract: Motivation loss is a transdiagnostic symptom, prevalent across neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. Current treatments fail to effectively treat this symptom domain, giving it significant clinical importance. The fields of neuroscience and drug development have primarily focused on extrinsic motivation, whereby an animal must perform an action to receive an external food or water-based reward. However, many of our everyday activities are facilitated by intrinsic motivation, where completing an action is inherently rewarding. By utilising tasks focused only on extrinsic motivation, we may miss critical neurobiological and therapeutic differences between motivation types. Previous work has shown divergence in drug effect between extrinsic and intrinsic motivation tasks across a wide range of clinically-used drugs, indicating translationally-relevant differences across motivation domains that warrant further study. Therefore, the aim of this work was first to develop a task capable of simultaneously quantifying intrinsic and extrinsically motivated behaviour within the same task environment. Secondly, to use this task to further investigate this neurochemical divergence by examining a wide range of clinically-relevant drugs within this new task context. Here, we find that a pharmacological reduction in dopaminergic signalling reduced motivation across both extrinsic and intrinsic options within the new task, though this effect was mechanism dependent. In contrast, acute serotonergic and dopaminergic signalling increase produced a more heterogenous pattern, indicating nuanced mechanistic differences even when presented in the same task environment. Therefore, this task provides a new approach for characterising drug effects on distinct forms of motivated behaviour that may go unnoticed using conventional assays.
